title: Historical records on Bigfoot sightings revisit tracks, doubts in Umatilla County
byline: Mark Rattner NonStop Local Digital Journalist
excerpt: PENDLETON, Ore. — New historical documents by the U.S. Forest Service detail a reported Bigfoot sighting in Umatilla County, sparking new interest among believers and skeptics alike.
content:
PENDLETON, Ore. — New historical documents by the U.S. Forest Service detail a reported Bigfoot sighting in Umatilla County, sparking new interest among believers and skeptics alike.

U.S. Forest Service records from 1982 show two investigators reached different conclusions after examining reported Bigfoot tracks in the Mill Creek watershed south of the Washington-Oregon border.

The documents, dated June 18 and July 26, 1982, describe a Forest Service wildlife biologist's inspection of tracks in the Low Creek drainage and a Border Patrol agent's separate opinion that the tracks were a hoax.

The wildlife biologist, Rodney Johnson, wrote that he accompanied a group into the Mill Creek Watershed on June 17 after being asked the day before to investigate a reported find of "Bigfoot" tracks.

He said the reported tracks were found at three locations, including sites along the Low Creek Trail and near the top of Low Ridge.

At Site "A," Johnson wrote, the group found six identifiable tracks in muddy trail conditions and made plaster casts of two of them.

At Site "B," he wrote, the group found about 18 prints over roughly 40 feet near a bog next to the trail and made casts of two more tracks.

Johnson wrote that the third site was not visited because of the time of day and conclusions reached at the second site.

In his conclusion, Johnson wrote that it was his opinion the tracks at Sites "A" and "B" were made by something other than "a 300 pound plus two footed being."

He said the stride did not change with slope, the tracks were not to the bottom of the mud and the toe markings were too clear.

Johnson also wrote that, if the tracks were faked, "someone went to a great deal of trouble and detail."

In the July 26 memo, Border Patrol agent Joel Hardin said the tracks were "a very clever attempt to perpetrate a hoax."

He wrote that the tracks in two separate locations were identical in appearance, size and individual characteristics and concluded they were made by the same "Bigfoot."

Hardin said the tracks appeared to have been made by some type of soft plaster or rubber coated boot.

He wrote that the tracks did not push down to solid material in soft mud, stayed "straight in line" and appeared and disappeared on the trail without signs leading to or away from the area.

Hardin said he believed the maker of the tracks was someone with normal access to the area who was knowledgeable and interested in "Bigfoot" legends and stories.

Over the last month, the U.S. Forest Service has released several historical documents on Bigfoot sightings around the country.
